speechtext:
The house resumed, from February 19, consideration of the motion of the Prime Minister :
That it is expedient that parliament do approve of the general treaty for the renunciation of war, which was signed at Paris, on the twenty-seventh day of August, nineteen hundred and twenty-eight, on behalf of His Majesty for the Dominion of Canada by the plenipotentiary named therein, and that this house do approve of the same.

speakeroldname: Mr. C. H. CAHAN (St. Lawrence-St. George):
subtopic: MULTILATERAL TREATY FOR THE RENUNCIATION OF WAR
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think it is the general opinion of the house and of the country as a whole that on memorable national and international occasions the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) has expressed his views and the views of Canada generally with dignity, with clarity, in concise and choice diction and with an eloquence that has merited and received the commendation of all. I refer to such memorable occasions as the dedication of the Peace tower, the celebration of the sixtieth anniversary of the foundation of this Dominion, the occasion of the signing of the peace pact at Paris, the recent address delivered before the League of Nations at Geneva and the somewhat memorable pronouncement which he made on the twenty-eight October last at Quebec, on his return from Paris, Geneva and London. I think the same commendation generally may be extended to his address on Tuesday last in advocacy of the adoption of the Paris peace pact in renunciation of war. I am sure the applause which attended his address, and that which followed the eloquent and inspiring address of the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) convinced the members of the house and the country generally that perfect unanimity of opinion prevails in Canada with regard to the ratification of this pact of peace. Therefore it is not in any cavilling spirit, not from any desire to make captious criticism, that, having moved the adjournment of the

International Peace-Mr. Cahan
debate, I desire to present one single issue in respect of this peace pact which I believe to be of vital significance to the future welfare of Canada, especially in its relation to the great republic to the south of us. The Prime Minister, in memorable words, on Tuesday last said:
In the name of the multitude of their dead, the nations that have signed this treaty have pledged their honour in the face of mankind never again to resort to war as a means of settling controversies between them. Surely, if there is such a thing as national honour existing, this treaty must hold a large place in the future of the world.
And then proceeding to describe the organization that had been attempted, tinder the covenant of the League of Nations, to ensure the future peace of the world, the Prime Minister -called attention to the fact that there were certain gaps still existing in that organization. He said:
In the first place, the League of Nations does not include within its membership all the nations of the world. The United States, which is a signatory to this treaty, is not a member of the League of Nations.
I desire to proceed this afternoon with the inquiry whether that gap is closed, and as to whether in view of the attitude of the government and of the predominating public opinion in the United States, that gap may he satisfactorily closed in the interests of permanent peace relationships between this country and that great republic. The Prime Minister touched upon that aspect of the question when he said:
It is obviously to the interests of Canada to have from her neighbours, from the countries that surround her, an assurance upon their national honour that never will resort be had to war as a means of settling any differences which may arise. That reason has been mentioned elsewhere as a prudential reason, a reason of prudence, if nothing else, why this country should become a party to a treaty of this kind. Canada is fortunate perhaps in her geographical position.
May I add to that, that Canada is fortunate in her geographical position only in so far as there prevails throughout the neighbouring republic, dominating its different public policies, the will to peace, not only with Canada, but the will to permanent peace with the great Britannic commonwealth of which we are members and with the great League of Nations, of which also we are members. The Prime Minister continued:
We have hut the one neighbour to the south, and this neighbour-
I am omitting some immaterial words:
-along with the other nations of the world, gives its solemn pledge that never for all time

to come will it resort to war as a means of settling any controversies that may arise.
Mr. Cahan: Does the right hon. gentleman understand that to be embodied in this document?
Mr. Mackenzie King: Most decidedly so. I cannot see how this document is capable of any other interpretation than that as between Canada and the United States-let me enlarge that-as between the British Empire and the United States. Neither will ever resort to war as a means of settling differences which may arise between them, but that they will settle all differences by pacific means, and to that end each has pledged its honour before the entire world.
I think that in the expression of that hope and aspiration touching the future relations of these great countries the Prime Minister voiced the sentiments not only of this house but of all the people of Canada. He was not more positive in his expression of opinion than was M. Briand at Paris, where, speaking in the presence of the assembled representatives of the signatory powers, he said:
Thus, shall war as a means of arbitrary and selfish action no longer be deemed lawful. Thus, its threat shall no longer hang over the economic, political and social life of peoples. Thus, shall the smaller nations henceforth enjoy real independence in international discussions. Freed from the old bondage, the nations that have signed the new contract will gradually forsake the habit of associating the idea of national prestige with the idea of force, and this single psychological fact will not be the leas* important factor in the evolution that is needed to lead to the regular stabilization, of peace.
That pact was signed at Paris on August 27th last by representatives of fifteen countries. By September 12th, 1928, I noticed in the public reports that three other nations had adhered to the pact., and twenty^-five others had signified their intention to adhere as soon as the constitutional means could be taken for ratification. Now I understand that all but three have indicated their adherence or intention to adhere, those three being Argentine, Brazil and Liberia.
I was very much struck indeed by the pronouncement made by the Prime Minister, at Quebec, I think, on his return. For myself, and speaking from my own ideals, I was impressed seriously with the hope that the pact of peace might prove to be all that the Prime Minister so ardently hoped for the nations that were giving adherence to it. But on November 1, last, an address was made in New York by a notable American, Mr. Houghton, who had been United States ambassador to- Germany, and who had just recently returned from being ambassador of the United States at the court of St. James, He had returned to his own country, and there, it would appear from the address, which

International Peace-Mr. Cahan
he gave on that date, that this spirit and will to peace which had encircled him in London was not finding expression in the public prints of his own country, and therefore he expressed himself as follows:
Until we, here in America, are ready to accept, in a practical sense, as fairly equivalent to our own, the goodwill and integrity of purpose and trustworthiness of other peoples, we shall find a durable peace beyond our reach. That is the obvious but unpleasant truth, and I know even to mention it tends to arouse all the cynical forces of distrust and suspicion within us. But there it is. It cannot be evaded!
In a world that is armed, we cannot go unarmed. In a world which is still mainly based on force, eventualities, no matter how insane, in themselves, must still be considered, and we do not need to exaggerate them. But to forget them wholly would be quite as bad. There are times, we must remember, when police power is as necessary in foreign affairs as in domestic affairs.
Upon reading that speech I felt a degree of apprehension that I find it difficult to express. November 11 was Memorial day. It is a day that is sacred to us in Canada, a day that we make a memorial for our dead, a day perhaps which is more engrossing to us in this country than to the people in the neighbouring republic, where owing to their enormously larger population the sacrifices through death and wounds which they made in the war came not so closely home to them as it did to our small population.
I remember my own feelings on November 11. I stood at the grave of my own son. Wounded in the war by shell fire, his spine partially shot away, paralyzed in his lower limbs, obtaining internal action of his organs only by mechanical means,, yet through severe suffering he attempted to overcome weakness and pain and to take some part again in the public service of his country. As I stood by that open grave and watched scores of his old companions in arms passing by, with their simple impressive rite of bidding hail and farewell by each throwing a maple leaf upon the open grave; young men, scores of them, halt and wounded, some whose faces bore ineradicable expressions of pain and suffering and sorrow, the most of them clad in heavy boots, wool jerseys -and rough jackets; young men from the fishing fleets, young men from the timber and lumber camps, young men from the farms-I felt in my own agony, God be blessed that this peace pact is in a way to be achieved as an aid and incentive t,o the preservation o.f the peace of this country and of the empire to which it belongs.
I was in that spirit when, two or three days later, I picked up the New York Herald-Tribune and read the address of the President
of the United States on November 11-the same day which is so sacred in the memories of many families in Canada. In that address he spoke first of the necessity of preparation for war, secondly, of the limitation of the armaments of war, and lastly, remember, of the renunciation of war for the achievement of national policy. I will read his words:
If the European countries had neglected their defences, it is probable that war would have come much sooner. All human experience seems to demonstrate that a country w'hich makes reasonable preparation for defence is less likely to be subject to a hostile attack and less likely to suffer a violation of its rights which might lead to war. This is the prevailing attitude of the United States and one which I believe should constantly determine its actions. To be ready for defence is not to be guilty of aggression." We can have military preparation without assuming a military spirit. It is our duty to ourselves and to the cause of civilization, to the preservation of domestic tranquillity, to our orderly and lawful relations with foreign people, j.) maintain an adequate army and navy.
We do not need a large land force. The present size of our regular army is entirely dequate, but it should continue to be supplemented by a national guard and reserves, and especially with the equipment and organization in our industries for furnishing supplies. When we turn to the sea the situation is different. We have not only a long coast line, distant outlying possessions, a foreign commerce unsurpassed in importance, and foreign investments unsurpassed in amount, the number of our people and the value of our treasure to be protected, but we are also bound by international treaty to defend the Panama canal. Having few' fuelling stations, we require ships of large tonnage, and having scarcely any merchant vessels capable of mounting five or six inch guns, it is obvious that, based on needs, we are entitled to a larger number of -warships than a nation having these advantages.
That is the pronouncement of the executive head of the great nation to the south of us, showing what confidence his government and the people that he represents had in the peace pact of Paris as an agency for securing the permanent peace of the world.
Now, is it any wonder that the New York Herald-Tribune-which I have read, I think, almost daily for thirty or forty years, and which to a large extent in its editorial columns is an expression of the views of the dominant political party of the United States -is it any wonder that this journal on November 13 last, in eulogizing the president's address from which I have read this extract said:
The United States is now the richest and most powerful nation in the world. It has, as the president pointed out, a foreign commerce unsurpassed in importance and foreign investments unsurpassed in amount. We have a long coast line and distant outlying possessions as well as our ow-n population and treasure to protect. This duty of defence comes first

By that I think the Prime Minister intended to suggest the entrance of the United States into the League of Nations, an event which always has appeared most desirable, or to revert to his words:

International Peace-Mr. Cahan
-or an adjustment of the old rules of neutrality to meet the new conditions of cooperative defence.
That is the real essence of the whole controversy, and I doubt if it could be more accurately expressed in diplomatic language. I understand and appreciate the reserve which the Prime Minister of Canada is bound to exercise in such a case, but as a simple, private member of His Majesty's opposition in this house I am not bound by the same restraints or reserves. Does the United States, under the guise of protecting its neutral rights, intend to flaunt the unanimous decision of the council of the League of Nations-because these decisions must be unanimous in this regard-and use its naval forces to preclude the members of the league from imposing economic pressure upon an outlaw power? Before developing that idea, however, let me quote further from the Prime Minister, who continued:
In any event, if, as would seem to be the case, the proposed multilateral treaty does not impose any obligation upon a signatory in relation to a state which has not signed the treaty or has broken it-
That is, in relation to a state which has not signed the Paris peace pact or which, having signed, has broken that pact, which is admittedly the crux of the controversy. Then the Prime Minister continued:
-any decision taken to apply sanctions against a member of the league which has made war in violation of its covenant pledges would not appear to conflict with the obligation of the treaty.
That is, it would not be in conflict with the obligations which the Paris peace pact imposes upon those who are parties to the covenant of the League of Nations. In that conclusion I entirely concur, and under the circumstances it was doubtless inexpedient for the Prime Minister, in this diplomatic document, to proceed further and point out clearly that the most powerful financial and industrial nation of the world is not bound by the inhibitions which are imposed upon those who adhere to the covenant of the League of Nations. It alone, among the powerful nations of the world, is still free to recognize any power which is so outlawed by a declaration of the council and assembly of the League of Nations.
Let me refer to article 16, which goes further and provides that should any member of the league resort to war in disregard of its covenants, as specified, then it shall be deemed ipso facto to have committed an act of war against the other members of the league.

speechtext: Before putting the motion, Mr. Speaker-

subtopic: MULTILATERAL TREATY FOR THE RENUNCIATION OF WAR
speechtext:
I take it that the Prime Minister will close the debate if he speaks now, and I desire to offer two suggestions to the problem mentioned in the debate which has taken place in connection with this treaty. I am spurred by the generous tribute paid by the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Cahan), and wish to join with him in congratulating the Prime Minister on the excellent manner in which he represented the interests of the Canadian people overseas. I do not think anyone is insensible to the honour he has done not only himself but Canada as well in connection with these negotiations.
I also think both the Prime Minister and the leader of the opposition struck the right note when they suggested that without further efforts in the direction of peace the treaty itself would be almost useless. That reminded me of what Lord Grey wrote as an introduction to General Sir George Aston's book on the study of war. At that time Lord Grey wrote. I quote:
The third point of view, which is very important for all educational institutions, is that each generation should be brought up to realize what modern war means. In my boyhood we were all taught what war meant, but we regarded war as something very different from what we now know that it means; and it is by bringing home to each succeeding generation what the realities of modern war are, how vastly more castrophic and disastrous it is to the whole population than ever before, that we shall form a public opinion which will help to secure peace. It is, therefore, especially essential that the study of war in all educational institutions should be brought up to the point of bringing home to each generation what modern war really means, in order that we may have, in succeeding generations, a public opinion, not only in this country, but in other countries, which understands that it is to the interest of nations that they should avoid such things as the last war. The study of war would show that any future war will be even more disastrous and destructive to human life and property than the great experience we have all been through.
Applying the above to the present discussion I submit that it would not be carrying out the suggestion of Sir Edward Grey, and all other statesmen, if we were to allow this debate to conclude without doing our best to show the people who study the question just what is and is not involved in the treaty itself.

International Peace-Mr. Garland (Bow River)
I am not going to criticize captiously, but I do wish to point out that while we feel we can ratify this treaty, which is a step forward in the direction of international amity, yet there are conditions surrounding it which circumscribe and contract it, and about which the people should know if our further efforts in the direction of peace are to be fruitful. Strictly speaking, the treaty itself did not originate with either Briand or Kellogg. If I remember correctly, the first rought draft of a treaty of this type was produced by Professor Shotwell of Columbia university. The draft was brought to the attention of Senator Borah and also of Nicholas Murray Butler, the president of Columbia university. Both these men were so taken with the possibilities of such a treaty and it appealed to their imaginations so effectively that they took steps to see that M. Briand in France secured a copy of this draft. I think we should indicate to the professor during the course of this debate that we know it was neither Briand nor Kellogg who originated this idea, but that the present draft was his own work. This treaty has been referred to as the greatest event the world has seen since the birth of Christ. Of course, we know to-day that that is a wild emotional outburst having little basis in fact.
There are unquestionably reservations surrounding it which unquestionably detract from its force. The Prime Minister has said there are none; that he preferred to adopt the verbiage of Mr. Chamberlain and to intimate that there were no reservations to the treaty. But the right hon. gentleman intimated that there Were "interpretations," and in the final analysis it is the interpretations of the treaty, if accepted, that become the treaty. I think the Prime Minister knows very well that the treaty is circumscribed; it is contracted from the original form in which it went out by certain proposals. After the proposed treaty was submitted to France by Mr. Kellogg, France led the European concert in the direction of reservations, subsequently accepted by the United States. The first suggestion was that there should be an amendment to the draft of the treaty leaving wars of self-defence outside the ban imposed by it. The second suggestion was that the violation of the treaty by one of the signatories released all the others, and the third suggestion reserved any commitments that had been made by the respective signatories under the covenants of the league or other pacts such as the Locarno pact and the treaties of neutrality. The treaties of neutrality are rather important
from the European point of view, inasmuch as it is through them there has been established what is now known as the "little entente"; a growing and powerful factor in European affairs.
Mr. Oliver Cabot Lodge, in an article in Harpers magazine for December last, commented upon the interesting situation which arose; the following appears at page 34:
The State Department thought that if these amendments were secured, there would be nothing left of the Kellogg proposal. A high official of the department told the writer, for instance, that if these points were even admitted the treaty would be made "ridiculous." But here is what finally happened. The treaty itself was not amended, but the French points were virtually admitted by Secretary Kellogg in his address before the American Society of International Law in Washington on April 28, 1928.
The article continues:
But in this case it was felt that the sole value of the treaty lay not in its binding effect -which admittedly is practically nil-but in the "moral" effect which the knowledge of its existence would have on public opinion which, it was hoped, would be very great. Therefore, it was argued, the special interests of the parties concerned would be adequately cared for if they were incorporated in diplomatic notes, provided that these notes received the same attention from the public as did the treaty itself.
This is contrary to the usual manner of restricting treaties by amendments. Because of the very nature of this treaty Mr. Lodge submits that it was only necessary to agree to the terms of certain diplomatic "notes" to have the treaty in effect amended although not changing the wording of it. The article continues:
It thus follows that these reservations demanded by France are actually, if not legally, co-equal with the pact itself. But the senate will not pass on them.
He was disappointed in this regard, which brings us to another interesting point a little later on.

aware there were two gentlemen of international reputation both named Henry Cabot Lodge. The senator died some time ago, his son I believe wrote the article.
Mr. Lodge did not expect the senate to pass upon these reservations, but a powerful bloc consisting of from twenty-five to thirty senators opposed the treaty asking that the report of the committee be accompanied by a complete statement of the Monroe doctrine of the United States, and also that their position should be made very clear with respect to commitments in regard to obligations imposed by the treaty.
Brief reference to the report of this committee was made by the member for St. Law-rence-St. George (Mr. Cahan), but I think at this stage it would be better to refer first to the statement made by Mr. Chamberlain, who said that the real efficiency of the pact would depend not on any engagement undertaken by the United States government but on how the rest of the world thought the United States government would judge the action of an aggressor, and whether they would help or hinder him in his aggression. In discussing this treaty in the House of Commons on July 30, Mr. Chamberlain said:
If the American nation ranges itself behind its own treaty, then indeed the signature of the treaty will be an additional and most formidable deterrent of war, and it will be in addition a most valuable security for peace.
According to Mr. Chamberlain, the real efficiency of this treaty is concurrent upon the United States definitely accepting obligations in regard to violators of the treaty. What did the senate of the United States do? It backed away altogether from that and all the eloquence and power of Borah and those associated with him were powerless against the blockade. All the efforts of the pacifist movement in the United States were powerless against the opposition in the senate. They might not be powerless at a future time under other conditions and I would not like the impression to remain that was possibly left on the house by the hon. member for St. Law-renee-St. George (Mr. Cahan) that the senate was expressing the will of the people of the United States. Certainly the minority group of twenty or thirty in the senate were not, in

my opinion, expressing the real will to peace that we find everywhere permeating the United States common people. But we do find that those few men in that powerful assembly were capable of having embodied as a part of their report on the treaty that which Mr. Lodge says, in a subsequent statement on the matter, ties the report definitely to the treaty itself and makes it an interpretation of the treaty. As they have included President Monroe's message of December 2, 1823, it might not be amiss at this stage to repeat it:
W: owe, it therefore, to candour and to the amicable relations existing between the United States and those powers to declare that we should consider any attempt on their part to extend their system to any portion of this hemisphere as dangerous to our peace and safety. It is impossible that the allied powers should extend their political system to any portion of either continent without endangering our peace and happiness.
So much for that. The report then continues :
The committee-
That is the foreign relations committee of the United States senate.
-further understands the treaty does not provide sanctions, express or implied. Should any signatory to the treaty or any nations adhering to the treaty violate the terms of the same, there is no obligation or commitment, express or implied, upon the part of any of the other signers of the treaty to engage in punitive or coercive measures as against the nation violating the treaty.
That interpretation of the position of the United States by the United States senate over the opposition even of Senator Borah is more eloquent than any criticism of the treaty by anybody else could in effect be. But that is not all. Let us go back again to Sir Austen Chamberlain's speeches. He says: The real efficiency of the treaty is the recognition by the United States of its obligations in respect thereto. The United States rejects any real obligations in respect thereto and, therefore, if Sir Austen Chamberlain's position be correct, surely the real efficiency of the treaty is destroyed. I do not think it really is, but I think a powerful supporting influence has been removed by the action of the United States senate.
Let us consider just another point in connection with this. So much for the United States Monroe doctrine, but if one listens to the speech of the hon. member for St. Law-rence-St. George coupling the Monroe doctrine with the expressed attitude of the United States to-day as he uttered it through the particular selections he made, one would imagine that the United States of America was the sole violator of this will to peace that the

International Peace-Mr. Garland (Bow River)
people of the world have so rapidly generated during the last few years. What are the facts? The very first suggestion that any doctrine similar to the Monroe doctrine should become a part of or be a circumscribing regulation to the treaty came, not from the United States who sent the draft treaty in its original form and who were certainly prepared to sign it in its original form, but from England herself, in Sir Austen Chamberlain's letter, comes the restriction which has already been read by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth). Let me remind the house of its terms:
I should remind Your Excellency-
That is Mr. Kellogg.
- -that there are certain regions of the world the welfare and integrity of which constitute a special and vital interest for our peace and safety. His Majesty's government have been at '"mins to make it clear in the past that inter-c rence with these regions cannot be suffered. Their protection against attack is to the British Empire a measure of self-defence. It must be clearly understood that His Majesty's government in Great Britain accept the new treaty upon the distinct understanding that it does not prejudice their freedom of action in this respect.
The effect of that letter, of that interpretation, was at once to establish a definite British Monroe doctrine clearly and unequivocally. What could the United States people do; what could the United States senate do, faced by a situation in -which Sir Austen Chamberlain, speaking for the British people, said that the principle of self-defence shall not be confined even to the far-flung territories of the British Empire, but shall extend beyond them into unspecified regions, the location of which we have not yet been able to determine.
They may be Abyssinia, Persia, Egypt, or many other countries in which England has a special and [DOT] financial interest. Some of them are in Asia, some in Africa, and naturally her interests of defence in Europe are recognized. Therefore the British doctrine laid down by Sir Austen Chamberlain's letter deliberately destroys the influence of the treaty if the principle of self-defence is not narrowed down and more clearly defined with respect to the continents of Europe, Asia and Africa. The United States Monroe doctrine destroys the effect of the treaty in respect of the American continent, and the only other one left is Australia, which, as part of the British commonwealth, would be involved in any difficult situations arising out of such reservations if accepted. One could go on and discuss this question of the Mon-roe doctrine and the British policy in regard thereto at some length.
I do not wish t-o do that, but I would direct
-the 'attention of the Prime Minister to the Manchester Guardian of -May 25 last, in which appears a leading editori-al o-pposing Sir Austen's extension of the right of selfdefence to cover "certain regions" outside the empire which are of "special and vital interest to our peace and safety". Further it says:
The treaty outlawing war should not be allowed to become a vehicle for setting up a "British Monroe doctrine," says the Guardian.
Certainly there is no question about the position of the liberal-minded persons of Great Britain in that -respect. It was voiced by the Manchester Guardian in no uncertain terms. Then Lord Cecil rose in the House of Lords and attempted to secure a definition from Lord Cushendun as to just where these territories were, what the areas were, what the particular interests were; but he received no satisfaction whatever to his inquiries, nor has anyone since been able to clear up just what these unspecified territories are. To quote further:
"The oddest result of all," says the Manchester Guardian, concerning the treaty discussion, "would be that acceptance of the treaty by Great Britain should be made the occasion for asserting her right, even though she should not herself be attacked, to wage war in certain as yet unspecified regions of the world, which are of special and vital interest to her."
Mr. THOR-SON:	Would the hon. member
say that Canada associates herself with that interpretation by Sir Austen Chamberlain?

A going
around, enfilading. Wh-at is this thing that they call self-defen-ce? Great Britain has spoken of it; the United States has spoken of it.
The right hon. the Prime Minister referred I think to Lord Cushendun's remarks the other day in which he qualified it as " bona fide self-defence." What is bona fide selfdefence? It is just as vague as the other. It is just as ridiculous, really, as the other, and it does not in any degree safeguard us, nor can we be safeguarded until there is a very clear definition of just exactly what is

International Peace

Mr. Garland (Bow River)
meant by self-defence. Before I go any further I want to quote Doctor Morrison of the Christian Century, in this regard:
It is beginning to be evident that the British reservation is sabotaging the pact, that it leaves a huge gap in the renunciation of war-indeed, for Britain the gap is bigger than the renunciation-and that it practically invites the defeat of the pact in the United States senate.
I submit that opinion to the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Cahan), who is bitterly critical, and with some justification, of the United States militaristic preparations. There is no question about it, there is some justification for these criticisms, but there also has been some provocative action on the part of Great Britain. Doctor Morrison goes on:
But this British reservation has confused the issue. It has introduced "ifs and ands." Thus our senate has been provided with a smokescreen-
Indeed it has:
-behind which it can completely emasculate the treaty.
Professor Edwin M. Borchard of Yale, one of the leading American jurisconsults, writes:
Tlie treaty as now qualified by the French and British reservations constitutes no renunciation or outlawry of war, but, in fact and in law, a solemn sanction for all wars mentioned in the exceptions and qualifications. When we look at the exceptions, we observe that they nclude wars of self-defence, each party being free to make its own interpretation as to when self-defence is involved, war under the League Covenant, under the Locarno treaties, and under the French treaties of alliance. If self-defence *mild be limited to the terms "to defend its territory from attack or invasion," as suggested by Mr. Kellogg, it would be of some value, but it is understood that no specific definition of self-defence is necessarily accepted.
I simply submit the evidence of these authorities upon that one point of self-defence to show how it vitiates the whole treaty and almost destroys its effect unless we are willing, as has been expressed in this house already, to go on now and endeavour to secure a closer and a better definition of just what self-defence does actually mean. I might by the way in this regard quote a rather facetious utterance of Lloyd George. Mr. Lloyd George discusses this question at some length in his articles in the Daily Express. He says:
The rejoicing amongst genuine advocates of a peace based on judgment and not on violence has been abated considerably by the reservations demanded by France (re-echoed by Britain) and accepted by Kellogg in his famous speech. They realize the advantage of a solemn declaration by all the great powers condemning war as an instrument of national policy. But their doubts may be expressed in this form:
I am satisfied that this will appeal to the hon. member for Cartier (Mr. Jacobs):

"Thou shalt not kill", was a definite commandment which had a legal as well as a moral force. But supposing Moses, in order to pro-pitate the most contentious tribes, had delivered an allocution to the children of Israel explaining that he had not quite meant the inhibition to be taken too literally, and that its operation must be subject to considerable qualifications- that killing to protect certain interests was permissible, and that if you killed in self-defence, you were the sole judge of what constituted rdf-defence. The practical value of the commandment would be seriously damaged by these modifications.
I think even the hon. member for Cartier would agree with him in that regard. We can see that the "interpretations" by no means help the pacific purpose of the treaty, and if those who so ardently support it are sincere, they must go much further than we have yet gone. We must go to the point of recommending a very clear definition of self-defence.

speechtext: The hon. gentleman is no doubt aware that the Germans still maintain that the Great war was one of self-defence on their part.

subtopic: MULTILATERAL TREATY FOR THE RENUNCIATION OF WAR
speechtext:
Quite right, and I have never discovered any major war in history that was not claimed to be one of salf-defence by both sides.
I have not very much time left, and although there is much to be said on this question I must curtail my remarks. The hon leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) made a very eloquent appeal the other day on this subject, and said that if we were sincere in the matters we should go further than the treaty and do our best to secure international disarmament. So strongly did he emphasize that point that he returned to it nine times in the course of his short speech, and in more eloquent terms than I command he laid before the house the dangers of armament, the terrible disasters that were likely to follow from having armies and navies and the countries simply waiting for an opportunity to use them. I do not need to quote the New York Nation in this regard, although it has an intensely interesting comment on the subject. All I will say is this: In dealing with the question of disarmament, we are dealing with a tremendously intricate problem. We are dealing with national jealousies, hatreds, fears, aspirations; we are dealing with the injustices perpetrated under the treaty of Versailles; we are dealing with many problems which we in this country have but the smallest conception of, and above all, we are dealing with chancelleries whose whole mental machinery has descended to them from, or has been constructed out of, the old

International Peace-Mr. Mackenzie King
policies of the past when treaties were made for the purpose of successfully waging war, not for the purpose of establishing peace, and until we can secure in the chancelleries of these countries persons who are pledged to peace and have the spirit and the will for peace, it is going to be a very difficult problem for us to solve. The only thing we can do is to do our best to solve it. Sir George Aston in his book on war, uses these terms:
The march of science has brought the whole human race into such close relationship that the life of every man, woman and child is intimately affected by conflicts.
No one questions that. The leader of the opposition reiterated it again and again in his speech, and I say that there is more hope for peace in the growing realization by all peoples of the truth of this statement of Sir George Aston's, the realization that any future major war will leave no part of the country free from the possibility of attack, but will expose every citizen, whether he be a prime minister or a preacher, a school teacher or a school boy, an inmate of a hospital or an old men's home, to being brought into actual personal contact with the conflict-there is more hope, I say, in the growing realization of that truth than there is in this pact of peace. Indeed, I will go this far and say that the pact of peace is an attempt to crystallize into definite form that realization which has been growing for the last ten years in the hearts of all people. No brush, Mr. Speaker, CGuId paint the horrors that will face civilization should we permit another major conflict to ensue. No words could describe, no imagination could even picture what is likely to occur. I therefore urge that in further pursuing this matter, the government of this country should, in addition to endeavouring to secure a proper definition of self-defence, go to the length of doing its best to be effective' by sending out an invitation to Great Britain and the other nations of the British commonwealth of nations and to the nations of the world to hold a disarmament conference. Do not wait for somebody else to do it; let us do it. Let the Prime Minister add still further to the laurels he has already gained by taking the first step in this direction.
Let us hold the conference here in Ottawa, far from the evil influences of London, Washington, Paris or any of those centres of the old diplomatic school. Let us make an appeal to the peoples of the world to come to us, one of the most peaceful nations on earth, with the greatest record of peace that I think any nation has, with a marvellous country to
show them, and let us demonstrate to them as clearly as we can our willingness to implement this treaty by real work. Faith? Yes. An expression of faith, say the Prime Minister. An expression of faith, says the leader of the opposition. But faith without works is dead. Let us now go to work. There should be little difficulty in inspiring the imagination of statesmen like my right hon. friend, like Premier Briand, like Secretary Kellogg, like ex-Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald. Others may not readily do so, but these men will respond. Then let us hold the conference free from the entanglements of experts, naval and military, except in an advisory capacity. Even there I would limit rigidly their powers in the course of the discussions.
Let us do this and so give the world that is struggling onward some real realization of the desire for an international civilized social order somewhat akin to the social order now definitely established within each state. Surely if the mind of man is sufficiently brilliant to conceive of these marvellous engines of production and of transportation that have so limited the area of the earth that to-day it is simply a matter of hours to span it, surely I say it can conceive and do for us that which must be done if we are to save our civilization.

Mr. Speaker, it is not my purpose in closing the debate to prolong in any particular the discussion which has taken place. I have rather in view a desire to give expression, on behalf of the government, to our appreciation of the tone of the debate throughout, to express satisfaction with the high level on which it has been maintained, of the sincerity with which hon. members from their different points of view have dealt with this alil-important subject; and above all to say that I agree most heartily with the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Cahan) when he says that there is one thing at least about which there can be no doubt, and that is the perfect unanimity with which this House of Commons gives its approval to the treaty itself.
One or two references have been made by the last speaker (Mr. Garland) to the question of reservations. I do not wish to go into that subject at the moment, but I would point out to him with respect to the so-called Chamberlain reservations, that since the time Sir Austen Chamberlain made the statement that there were certain regions which Great Britain regarded as vital, and which could not be attacked without her feeling that a
i6	COMMONS
International Peace-Mr. Mackenzie King
question of self-defence might present itself, practically all the nations of the world have signified their intention of adhering to the treaty. What powers Sir Austen Chamberlain may have had in mind as the ones likely to attack the regions to which reference has been made, I cannot say. I am quite certain, however, that they were not the one or two countries of South America which up to the present time have not signified their intention of adhering to the treaty. The fact that all countries now have virtually signified their intention so to do makes it quite evident that the so-called reservation at_ one time made by Sir Austen Chamberlain is no longer a matter of any significance, inasmuch as if one of these countries, or any country adhering to the treaty, is attacked by an aggressor, immediately other countries are relieved from their obligations under the treaty not to resort to war. So far, therefore, as the reservation made by the Secretary of State for Foreign Affairs of Great Britain is concerned, having regard to the present position of the treaty, I think, we may say, as Sir Austen Chamberlain himself did say, that Britain's adherence is given without any reservation.	.
It is always a difficult matter to interpret what may be in the minds of individuals or of nations. I doubt if any of us are justified in judging other individuals or other nations. I think we are safe if we continue to hold that "By their fruits ye shall know them," and if we believe that the nations which have signed this treaty have done so believing in their hearts that they ^ were helping to mark a place of new beginning in the relations towards each other of the nations of the earth. That place of new beginning will, without question, have its effect upon international law. International law, like everything else, is a matter of growth, of evolution. International law, in years gone by, was based upon the theory that war might be an instrument of national policy, that it had a certain legitimacy, that it was an attribute of national sovereignty. That can now no longer be asserted of war. War has lost its legitimacy, it has lost any association with the sovereignty of nations, it has become a thing that is abhorred and outlawed so far as the world is concerned, and from now on the nations of the earth will seek through the medium of international conferences and in other ways so to restate or develop the underlying principles of international law that instead of their being based on any theory of the possible exercise of force as a legitimate sanction on the part of nations in their relation with each other they will have to be based on some theory of the settlement

of all international controversies by pacific means. I believe in that particular a great advance has been made, and I am sure that we shall see at the League of Nations and at other international conferences efforts made for disarmament, for arriving at understandings between countries as to the governing principle in such matters as the freedom of the seas, efforts to lay down a new course of procedure, not entirely new perhaps, but at all events of a character which will beget an adherence to understandings, to principles and to obligations surih as has not been possible heretofore.
May I say to my hon. friend who has just spoken that I think we are indebted to him for having brought into the discussion the name of Professor James T. Shotwell. It had been my intention to make reference to Professor Shotwell, because without knowing how far my hon. friend may be justified in all he has said, I feel certain that those who know most about this treaty would be the first to concede that Professor Shotwell's part had been an all important one. Without doubt the best treatise on the question of war as an instrument of national policy, on the Briand-Kellogg peace pact, is the volume which I hold in my hand, and which is entitled War as an Instrument of National Policy and its Renunciation in the Pact of Paris, by James T. Shotwell. The fact that Professor Shotwell, now a professor at Columbia university, is a Canadian and a graduate of Toronto university is I think a source of pride to us all.
With regard to Canada's position in the matter of reservations, that was made quite clear in the correspondence which was brought down. There was one feature about our reply to the invitation which was extended, a feature which distinguished it in one particular perhaps, from others that were received namely, it was the briefest and the most to the point. The communication in which Canada's reply was sent reads:

Sir,-I desire to acknowledge your note of June 23rd and the revised draft which it contained of the treaty for the renunciation of war, and to state that His Majesty's government in Canada cordially accepts the treaty as revised and is prepared to participate in its signature.
Accept, Sir, the renewed assurances of my highest consideration.
(Sgd.) W. L. Mackenzie King,
Secretary of State for External Affairs.

to say in regard to the work of the Department of External Affairs is that too much credit, where credit is due at all, cannot be given to the Under Secretary of State for External Affairs, whose quite exceptional talents and services we are so fortunate as to have at the present time. I refer of course, to Dr. O. D. Skelton.
There is just one word further I desire to say before I conclude. I should like to thank my hon. friend the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) for his kind congratulations upon the small part I played in representing Canada at the signing of the peace pact in Paris, and also to express to other hon. members in the different political parties my very sincere appreciation of the extremely generous way in which many of them have made reference to that part and to my presence at the League of Nations in Geneva. It was a great privilege and honour to have had the opportunity of representing Canada in the signing of a document as momentous as this treaty for the renunciation of war, and to have had the privilege of participating in a conference as memorable as that which was held ,at Paris. Great as was that honour and privilege, I am sure hon. members will believe me when I say that there is something which I shall always'cherish even more deeply. It is that in seeking to discharge my duty as the representative of Canada on that occasion, in the endeavour to give expression to what I believed to be the single mind of this country, I appear, if I am to judge by what has been said, not to have too greatly disappointed the expectations of some of my friends, and to have been so fortunate as to have won the kindly approval of my fellow members in this parliament.

Mr. Chairman, the only problem that we really have to deal with is that which is incident to competition between two great system of railways, and I suggested to the minister the other day, as I suggest to him now, that he is entitled to much congratulation on having been able to iron out the differences between the two great systems of transportation until to-day there is only one difference at issue. But there is a fundamental principle that I think this house should adopt in considering matters of this kind, and that is that the Canadian National system should be treated exactly as though it were a privately owned system;
C.N.R.-Branch Lines

that is, they should be treated in exactly the same way as the Interstate Commerce Commission would consider, for instance, an application by the Southern Pacific to invade the territory of the Santa Fe, or an application by the Santa Fe to build into Southern Pacific territory, so-called. Because we are owners of an enterprise, we must not treat that enterprise as though it were other than a privately owned company for the purposes of determining where lines should be built. There was a time when we had so-called spheres of influence amongst the nations of the world. It is alleged that there are spheres of influence with respect to transportation systems. I think probably that state of affairs will disappear as the country settles and we get more people, because it is obvious that as the population increases one system of transportation will never be satisfactory to densely settled communities; and under those conditions we cannot hope to maintain a monopoly, either for the privately owned road or for our own system.
When I went to western Canada there was but one system of railway operating in the provinces of Alberta and Saskatchewan, except some small subsidiary lines that were owned by others and operated by the Canadian Pacific. As population increased and traffic became denser, two other systems entered the field, the Canadian Northern and the Grand Trunk Pacific. Some of us ventured to point out that there was an endeavour to build many miles of railway in territory where the traffic would not support such additional lines. When we found an effort to duplicate the Canadian Northern system of that day by the Grand Trunk Pacific running from Winnipeg to Edmonton, we pointed out what the inevitable result would be. It is true we did not receive much commendation from the public for doing so, and certainly the electorate did not manifest any great enthusiasm for our suggestions. And yet we know that we had the absolute bankruptcy of two systems of railroad because this parliament guaranteed the securities of both in order that each might destroy the other. That is a historic fact.
Now, my hon. friend from Red Deer (Mr. Speakman) referred to the handicap that he thought the Canadian National System was under as compared with the privately owned system when projecting new lines. He forgets the fact that the people of this country build the one and not the other. He forgets that with respect to everyone of these lines now under consideration the credit of Canada builds it. Parliament has the estimate of 
price and the statement of mileage is submitted in order that we may understand exactly what our ultimate liability will be, because, as every thoughtful man knows, it is on the credit of Canada that the money is borrowed, and not on the credit of the railway system. Some of the branch lines projected, as the minister was good enough to say on previous occasions, are not lines that in themselves will be immediately productive, but they are built in order that that territory may receive needed transportation facilities even though at the outset a loss of money is involved. The country authorizes construction on the theory that you must, so far as possible, adjust those expenditures that transportation service may be rendered to all the people, and that wdiere large surpluses are derived in one particular locality some of the money may be available to take care of what it is hoped will not long continue a deficit in another locality.
The principle I think we should adopt in dealing with the introduction of a second system of railway into a territory that is already being served, is the principle that would govern if both systems were privately owned. That is the course we should follow in dealing with competition, because our failure to do so in the past brought about the bankruptcy of two systems of railway in this country. The country's credit was behind both of them. But the country's credit today is behind only one; and if the efforts that are being put forward to make this system self-supporting are to succeed we must treat these matters as business propositions. So far as I remember, I am not on the standing committee on railways, and I shall not be available for the purpose of assisting in any work the committee may do. But I do desire at this time, before the bills go to the committee, to record my views from the observations that I have made in western Canada, where most of the lines are being built and will be under construction during a series of years. Everyone knows what trouble, what quarrels, what bickerings, what misunderstandings arose as between race and race, as between creed and creed, as between province and province, because of the nonsensical clause 93 of the British North America Act, which had been framed in one way in Quebec, then

changed in the parliament of United Canada, and further changed in London.
