My hon. friend knows, of course, that I cannot guarantee the success of a negotiation between two parties. I could not say that the road would be taken over, because both the buyer and the seller are to be considered; and Sir Henry Thornton is in the same position in relation to that problem as with respect to others; he is empowered to undertake tentative negotiations with the owners, and upon being satisfied of the economic soundness of the proposition he may then make recommendations to the government and ascertain whether the government are prepared to accept. That position has not yet been reached

C.N.k.-Branch Lines
with respect to the Inverness road. I do not wish to convey to my hon. friend that it will not be reached, but at the moment I am not in a position to say definitely that it can be. It is a matter of bargaining.

I thank the minister for his explanation, but I would point out that this road is in a slightly different position from the others he has mentioned. Some four years ago the Canadian National system took this road over under lease although they did not buy it. They have been paying a rental of $25,000 a year for the road for the past four years and they have paid the owners something like $100,000. They hold the road under option to purchase at a price of, I believe, $500,000, and already they have paid, as I say, something in the vicinity of $100,000 or $125,000 in rental. The situation is this, that so long as they do not own the road, although they have already paid one quarter of the purchase price specified in the option, they will not improve it. My constituency is therefore in the unfortunate position of having the worst railroad service to be found in any part of Canada. If the Minister of Railways would travel over that road from Point Tupper to Inverness he would immediately experience a sensation which would be distinctly good for his soul. It seems to me that since the Canadian National have already paid over a quarter of the purchase price by way of rentals, the road should be taken over and brought up to the standard of a branch line in order to provide a suitable service for the people, some 35,000, whom the road serves. But this would be only an initial step, because after that we wish to have the road extended north about sixty miles to Cheticamp. My hon. friend laughs-
No, no.

-but I will te'l
him-
Just a genial smile.

-that if he ever comes to Inverness, as three of his distinguished colleagues did last year, to address a .political meeting, he will not laugh over this question. I do not think it is fair to the county which I represent and which is certainly one of the wealthiest in Nova Scotia and perhaps in the Dominion-that is, potentially. North of Inverness, in the sixty miles for which provision should be made in this program, we have something like two billion tons of coal. In Nova Scotia, when we speak of coal we speak generally in terms of the British Empire Steel Corporation, as though
there were no coal deposits in the province other than those controlled by that corporation. But in Inverness county we have as much coal as is controlled by the British Empire Steel Corporation, although we cannot develop it because of lack of transportation facilities. Now we want to see this road taken over by the government and extended north to Cheticamp.
I feel I owe the house no apology for speaking about this matter, even though it is of a local nature, because this is a principle which might be followed by parliamentarians in public life as well as by individuals in their private affairs:
To thine own self be true,
And it must follow, as the night the day,
Thou eanst not then be false to any man.
If we are true to the constituencies we represent in parliament, we cannot be false to any other part of Canada. I would strongly urge the minister to take over the Inverness road and then extend it north to Cheticamp. I listened this afternoon to that splendid eulogy of the Highlanders of Cape Breton from my very distinguished leader (Mr. Bennett), and naturally my Scottish pride was stirred. We all have our peculiar racial characteristics and are all inclined to think that our own race is the best in the worid. I must point out, however, that besides the Highlanders of Inverness county, to whom the leader of the opposition paid such a splendid tribute this afternoon, we have in the northern section, comprising 40 per cent of the population, about 15,000 French Acadians. Now if there is one class of people to whom Nova Scotia owes something, it is the French Acadian. He has been tried in the crucible and he came through splendidly. He has become a fine citizen of the province of Nova Scotia and of Canada, second to none in his loyalty to British institutions and in the love he always cherishes for this country and for that little plot he calls home. These are a homeloving people; the French Acadians in northern Inverness have stuck to the soil through thick and thin, through difficulties., travails and disappointments; they have stayed with agriculture and have developed homes for themselves under adverse circumstances.
Now what is the situation? In the winter some of these people have to carry their flour by team a distance of about fifty miles, and when they get a barrel of flour it costs them about S3 more than it costs any other Nova Scotian. That is a situation which should not prevail, and I think these people who have shown enough courage to remain on the land
C.N .k.-Branch Lines

and try to develop homes in this way while creating prosperity in the province of Nova Scotia are entitled to consideration from this government and from the Canadian National railways. I hope the day is not far distant when they will get the service they deserve, and if that service is not given by this government it will be given by the government headed by my leader after the next general election.

Perhaps I might deal
with this question before any others are addressed to me. I am sure my hon. friend will not charge the Canadian National railways with being unwilling to negotiate; I can assure him that the president of the system has made an offer for this property. Over a period of years the Canadian National railways have been paying a rental of $25,000 a year, I think, based on the interest on a capital sum, and I understood my hon. friend's remarks to indicate that he agrees that this rental is rather excessive. However, in this case I submit that the Canadian National management are in the best position to know what that property is worth to the Canadian National railways, and certainly I do not intend to say to the management that they must offer more than in their opinion is a fair price. I know an offer has been made; I have not in mind the figure, but surely my hon. friend should address his remarks to the owners of the property, or else have them iemonstrate from their point of view that any tentative offer made by the Canadian National management is not a fair offer. As my hon. friend indicated, the Canadian National railways now are giving service on the line in question, and I can assure him that for the last five years at least that service has been given at a loss with respect to the operation of that property. At all times the Canadian National railways have shown a disposition to endeavour to meet that situation as far as they could, having due regard to their responsibilities to the public as a whole.

I did not intend to criticize adversely the management of the Canadian National Railways in this regard; the reply of the minister was the first intimation I had that an offer had been made for the property. About a year ago I had a conversation with Sir Henry Thornton in his Montreal office, during which he told me that it was not a question of price at all, that the price of $500,000 in the option probably would be paid when the road was taken over. I did not know that an offer had been made since; all I wanted to get at was why the road has 
not been taken over. If it is a question of price and if the Eastern Trust Company, who own that road, will not come to terms, I think the Canadian National Railways could find some way of making them do so. If possible I would like to know what price has been offered the Eastern Trust Company.

I have not the price in mind, and in any case I think my hon. friend will agree that I have gone about as far as possible in giving information on a matter which is the subject of tentative negotiation. I am not anxious to embarrass the negotiations being carried on with respect to any of these properties; indeed, possibly the sounder course would have been to come to parliament only with such as have been concluded and to refuse to discuss those under negotiation. Knowing, however, my hon. friend's anxiety and the anxiety of other members from that part of the country I wanted to give the assurance I have given to-night. If my hon. friend can help in the negotiations he is free to do so.

It was gratifying to learn
from the Minister of Railways that an arrangement had been made between the two great railway companies with respect to the construction program for this year. I can assure the house that feeling is rather keen in Saskatchewan; they believe it unfair that in any part of that northern territory the Canadian Pacific Railway Company should run their lines across the trunk lines of the Canadian National Railways which have developed that part of the country at tremendous cost to Canada. I rose particularly to put on record the views of the organized farmers of Saskatchewan. In a short letter from Mr. Thrasher, he says:
Dear Sir:-	_	.	_
As you are aware, organized agriculture in western Canada for over twenty-five years has fought for the institution and protection of public ownership. We therefore urge that when the subject matter of the enclosed resolution is being considered by the federal government you give every consideration to the representations made herein.
The resolution, adopted by the United Farmers of Canada, Saskatchewan section, reads as follows:
Whereas we are advised that it is the intention of the Canadian national railways to pres-sent plans at the coming session of the federal parliament for their building program, and that such plans will include the construction of a branch line from Aberdeen to Melfort, and;
Whereas we believe the construction of such branch line will provide needed service to producers in that territory between Aberdeen and Melfort, and will form an integral part in the construction of the shortest possible transporta-

C.N.R.-Branch Lines
tion route from northern and central Saskatchewan to Fort Churchill via government railway lines,
Therefore be it resolved we strenuously urge upon the federal government that in justice to our own national railways, and for the protection of the producer and consumer from a transportation standpoint, the application of the Canadian National Railway for authority to construct a branch line from Aberdeen to Melfort be granted, such line to be constructed immediately authority is granted.
In short, that is the view of organized agriculture in the three prairie provinces. Resolutions similar to that have been passed repeatedly, particularly since 1904, when we asked for the government ownership of the terminal elevators at Fort William. We feel that now we are recovering from the railway debacle which faced us a short time ago we should not do anything to create such a situation again. Private ownership has been very costly to this country; in fact I think I would be quite justified in saying that no public utility in private hands has been a success in Canada. While it may have paid its way it has been too costly to the people, and the cost has been out of proportion to the return received by the producer.
These are some of the views which have been constantly brought forward by organized agriculture and deliberated upon year after year. We still believe that the logical thing for all public utilities in Canada is public ownership. While an arrangement is being made between the two railways as to their branch line program at this particular time, we feel that the fight is only beginning and that it will get keener and1 keener as the years go on. The time is not far distant when the people of this country will see that the railway situation-one company in private hands and the other under public ownership-will simply become unbearable. We have a board and general manager connected with the publicly owned system whom I believe the country can trust, but the time may come when this may not be the case, and we may have to step in and meet a situation as bad as the one of which we have rid ourselves.
I cannot allow this opportunity to pass without putting our views on record. I received a resolution from the Saskatoon board of trade in which they completely reverse the decision arrived at by the executive committee of that body some time ago. They now believe that while the Canadian Pacific Railway Company should be treated fairly it should not be allowed to cross the line of the Canadian National, but that running rights should be granted to the Canadian Pacific to permit them to get into the new territory. They suggest that the Canadian Pacific Railway Company
should acquire the line from Dalmeny to Carlton, and construct the parts needed to connect Saskatoon with Prince Albert. But whatever is done, I hope this parliament will not allow one railway to interfere with the earning power and the development and efficiency of service of the other.

As I understand it,1 the Canadian National not only receives authority from parliament to build lines, but that authority carries with it the obligation to build, whereas the charter received by the Canadian Pacific carries with it no obligation to build.
There is no obligation to build in any Canadian National bill, but there is an appropriation of money for a specific purpose, and of course it cannot be used for any other purpose.

I take it that when parliament votes the money for this purpose, the board of management of the Canadian National Railways can do nothing else but go ahead and spend that money as parliament dictates.
They must have a good reason for not going ahead; my hon. friend is right to that extent.

We know that companies have secured charters with the sole purpose of blocking the construction of other roads. The Canadian Pacific Railway Company has not been so great a sinner in this regard, but I do think the position of the two roads should be equalized. In certain cases the Canadian Pacific Railway charter should carry with it a forfeiture of bond and there would then be a direct obligation upon the company to go ahead and build the road, and the charter could not be used for the purpose of blocking another road.
The following is a resolution which was passed by the Wynyard section of the United Farmers of Canada:
Whereas, we believe that it is the earnest desire of the Canadian public that the national railways be allowed to expand consistently with the development needs of the country, that they may become an asset and not a liability and
Whereas it is becoming increasingly apparent that northern Canada will become a storehouse of revenue, and
Whereas, a competitive railway building program into these regions would not be to the best interest of the publicly owned railways,
Be it resolved; that we urge upon the Dominion parliament to give the national railway preference in allocating territory for railway building throughout the whole Dominion.
The following editorial appeared in the Winnipeg Free Press of January 12th last:
C.N.K .-Branch Lines

Having been the first in the field in the north, and being a publicly owned system in which the people of Canada have a large stake, the Canadian National system is entitled to something better than an even break in the allocation of the northern railway areas. This is to say, if both railways are prepared to build into a given area at the same time, the decision should go to the Canadian National.
The editorial continues:
The obvious line of policy for the Canadian National is to get in first, and we imagine the country will be prepared to deal with any government, house of commons, or senate, that gets in the way of this policy.
I think the principle laid down by the Free Press is a sound one, and whatever railway is in the territory should have the first opportunity to build there. The territory in dispute, as indicated by the Minister of Railways during the course of the debate this afternoon, is certainly Canadian National territory. I do not think any reasonable person will dispute that, and I hope when this matter comes before the railway committee that they will see that the Canadian National secures the consideration to which it is entitled.

Would the Minister of
Railways reply to the question asked by the hon. member for Brant (Mr. Smoke) this afternoon?

I apologize for having
overlooked replying to that question.

I am advised that this cut-off is intended solely for the use of through freight trains. With respect to other

related matters such as the cost of construction, the reasons for it, highway crossings and so forth, I am sure the two hon. members most interested will reserve their questions for the officers of the company in the railway committee. Just at the moment I have the general explanation that the reasons for the high cost per mile are the long, continuous deep cutting for a double track and two substantial highway crossings. Full details will be available for my hon. friends in the railway committee.

We have heard a good
deal this afternoon and evening with regard to giving each of the railways, the privately owned one and the publicly owned one, an equal opportunity. The trouble is that the publicly owned one, in my opinion, has not had an equal opportunity for a number of years. Prior to a year or so past I know that the amount of mail carried for the government by the Canadian Pacific was far more than that given to the Canadian National, and I only hope that by this time there has been a change in that respect. Again, lines which are constructed by the Canadian National are expected to be completed in three years. The Minister of Railways pointed out that there might be a discrepancy in the fact that while three years are given to the Canadian National, five years are given to the privately owned railway. The option of having two years to start and five years to finish may have been all right some years ago, but it is thoroughly out of date to-day, and we might quite well call for branch lines to be completed within three years, Railway building has developed tremendously of late years, as we have been shown in the very rapid development of the Hudson Bay railway; we should therefore equalize conditions between the two railways by having the same terms given to both with regard to construction.
I feel very much in sympathy with those members who have suggested that privately owned railways should be asked to put up some sort of security as a guarantee that they will go ahead with their work. Not only is it unfair to parliament that the railway company should fail to carry out the construction work for which a charter is given, but it is particularly unfair to those parts of Canada where the charters are given. I remember in 1922 the Canadian Pacific Railway Company came back for a charter for the eighteenth year. When a charter is given to a railway company the people very often flock into the district affected, in many instances by

C.N.R.-Branch Lines
the hundred, in anticipation that the railway is going to be built, and if construction is not gone on with for a number of years, frightful hardships are entailed on those who have settled there. It seems to me, therefore, that we should cut down to three years the time given to the railways to complete construction, and at the same time we should give the railways an equal opportunity for carrying His Majesty's mails.

Will there be an opportunity later in the session to discuss the question of branch lines? In this connection may I say that for the past three years I have brought to the attention of the house and particularly to that of the Minister of Railways the acquiring of a branch line about twelve or fifteen miles in length, owned by the Maritime Coal, Railway and Power Company, and running from Maccan to Joggins Mines in the county of Cumberland. I have been assured by the minister that the matter of acquiring it was under the serious consideration of his department.

No, of the management
of !he Canadian National.
Mr. SMITH' (Cumberland):	By implication at least some assurance has been given that this road will be taken over by the Canadian National. I do not think that is a very fair or frank manner of dealing with pleas such as have been in the past in this connection. The hon. member for Inverness to-night stated that the line he spoke of was, he thought, the worst in Canada. I think that is right with one exception; because this line to which I refer is even worse than the one of which he spoke. There is no objection on the part of the company owning the line to its being acquired at a reasonable price. It serves a country that is very rich in coal, agriculture and lumber. The people have pressed for consideration for the past number of years and the minister has given me to understand, through his answers in the house in previous years, that consideration would be given to the acquiring of this branch line. I do not think it is fair or frank for that sort of statement to be held out to those people when year after year large appropriations are asked for in connection with expenditures in other parts of Canada-and I have not the least objection to them-while these people are left with a totally inadequate railway system to serve that part of the county I have the honour to represent. Will the minister assure me that there will be some
opportunity of discussing the matter later on in the session, either when the railway estimates are brought down or on some other occasion ?

I cannot deny nor would 1 attempt to deny to my hon. friend the right to speak to this question at any time when, under the rules of the house, a matter of this kind may be discussed. In connection with his charge of lack of frankness, there are two sides to a bargain; there are buyers and sellers, and the Canadian National Railway is not compelled to deal with anyone with respect to the purchase of the line, is not compelled to pay the price that somebody thinks the line is worth. If my hon. friend has any information as to offers that have been made by parties owning the line in question and as to the public necessity of it, seeing that he is not satisfied with the answers he has hitherto received, I wish he would put down his arguments in a letter to me which I shall be glad to transmit to the management as representing his views so that there will be no misunderstanding between us in future. If my hon. friend regards my previous replies as being unfair and lacking in frankness, as he states, that is the only recourse I have. I cannot go further than that.

I have no
direct knowledge myself of the offer, or of anything concrete with respect to the negotiations that have taken place between the company and the Canadian National Railways; but my information is that they have been for some time past at the point of agreement, and that they are merely waiting for the Canadian National Railways to accept the offer which they have made and which they consider to be a reasonable one. As I say, I have not been in communication with the company and I cannot give any direct statement about the matter, but that is the information that comes to me from fairly reliable sources.

My hon. friend is of
course not the only member of the house who has pressed that matter of the Joggins railway. I cannot add anything to what I said a few moments ago.

In view of the observations of the Minister of Railways and Canals with regard to the purchase in the very near future of the Kent Northern Railway, I desire to draw his attention to the fact that in the last request made for its purchase a provision was embodied that in the event of its purchase favourable consideration should be given for its extension from Richibucto to St. Louis,
C.N.R.- Branch Lines

a distance of about seven miles. This extension would be of the greatest importance to the people of the northern section of Kent county, as it would serve one of the most beautiful and prosperous agricultural sections in New Brunswick. It is because of the disadvantages under which these people are labouring, and because of the advantages they would derive from the affording of proper railway facilities, that I take this opportunity of bringing this very important matter to the attention of the Minister of Railways. I trust, therefore, that at as early a date as possible after the negotiations have been completed he will ask the management of the Canadian National Railways to give the matter favourable consideration so that steps may be taken looking to the completion of the extension to which I refer.

I think it would facilitate business if the house would consent to have the bills read a second time now, in order that they might be immediately sent to the committee on railways and canals. The discussion we have had this evening is the sort of discussion which would normally take place on the second reading, and if the house is agreeable I would appreciate advancing the bills to that extent.
So far as we are concerned we desire to expedite the business of the house to that extent. There is no purpose to be served by delay, except delay itself, which wc do not desire.
Then I move, Mr. Speaker, that the said bills be now read a second time.

I doubt whether the
motion should be put in just that way. I think there should be a separate motion for each bill.

They will be recorded
separately. That was the understanding on a former occasion.
By unanimous consent.

speechtext: Mr. Chairman, this resolution deals with one feature only of a general amending bill covering several amendments to the railway act. speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I am glad indeed to hear the minister say that $200,000 a year for ten years will be provided for in the estimates. I desire to call to his attention an unsatisfactory condition of affairs in my constituency. A few years ago in the city of Moncton an arrangement was made with the railways for the depression of the railway tracks in order to eliminate the level crossings through the centre of the city. At that time the city council, influenced very largely by the press then supporting the Liberal opposition, declined to cooperate with the railway department. The railway went so far as to say they would pave the street between the two subways, as it was considered important that the work should be carried out. I wish to call the attention of the minister to the very urgent necessity of making those improvements. We have had some very near 78594-28
accidents at that point. Moncton, being the headquarters of the Intercolonial railway, is a very important railway centre, with upwards of 2,000 employees, and the Atlantic division of the Canadian National is handled there.
As this suggestion has been before his department on a previous occasion and has been approved, I would ask the minister to have it looked'into again to see if something cannot be done to improve these very unsatisfactory railway crossing conditions in the city of Moncton.

subtopic: GRANT TO RAILWAY GRADE CROSSING FUND
speechtext: Will the statistics which the minister proposes to pvt on Hansard show the number of people whom we are succeeding in killing on level crossings each year?

subtopic: GRANT TO RAILWAY GRADE CROSSING FUND
speechtext: In fairness to the railways I would say that it is a statement of the number of people who succeeded in killing themselves rather than of those whom the railway succeeded in killing. If there is one fact that is emerging from the investigations that are being conducted by the Board of Railway Commissioners with the aid of the municipalities and the safety league, it is that the people engage in the business of killing themselves to a far greater extent than the railways engage in killing them. A member of the railway board called my attention to this strange condition, that with respect to all the level crossings within our cities over which electric cars travel at very high speeds, the accidents are relatively few. I suppose it is because the danger is ever present within a city, whereas the temptation out on the country road is to try to beat the train. It seems to me that either the railway committee or some other committee, at any rate somebody, by means of a private resolution or otherwise, should bring this question to the attention of the house. I am informed by railway men that it is becoming a serious question for railway engineers. It is getting on their nerves, this foolish practice indulged in by some people who drive automobiles.
